title: The teaching of the Buddhas
hookLine: a kid in the back seat wants the whole path in one sentence; one verse has it
tomorrow: a chant of praise that says don't take its word. why?

cards: School pickup. The line of cars hasn't moved in five minutes, and the eight-year-old in the back seat is out of snacks and full of questions. So what is Buddhism?
In one sentence. Go. The parent at the wheel opens their mouth, and nothing short comes out.
Meditation, kind of. Karma, sort of. Not exactly a god.
The car ahead finally rolls forward. Here's the thing: the tradition has a verse built for exactly that moment, four short lines in Pali that monks and grandparents can say from memory.

teach.h: SABBAPAPASSA AKARANAM: NOT DOING ANY EVIL.
teach.b: Line one: sabbapapassa akaranam. Sabba, all. Papa, evil, the harmful thing done.
Akaranam, not-doing. Not doing any evil. Notice it starts with a not: before anything grand, stop adding harm.

teach.h: KUSALASSA UPASAMPADA: TAKING UP THE GOOD.
teach.b: Line two: kusalassa upasampada. Kusala is the skillful, the wholesome; upasampada is taking it up, arriving at it. Taking up the good.
Now there's something to do, not only something to skip. Line three: sacittapariyodapanam. Sa-citta, your own mind; pariyodapanam, making it clear, washing it clean.
Clearing your own mind. Your own, not your neighbor's.

teach.h: ETAM BUDDHANA SASANAM: THE BUDDHAS' TEACHING.
teach.b: Line four: etam buddhana sasanam. Etam, this. Buddhana, of the Buddhas, plural.
Sasanam, the teaching. Max Müller's old translation runs: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
He chose sin for papa, an English word with a long history of its own; the Pali sits closer to harm, the bad thing done. And keep an eye on that plural.
In the verse, this isn't one teacher's private rule; it's what awakened ones teach. So, back to the car. Stop the harm.
Take up the good. Clear your own mind. It fits between two traffic lights, and it holds a whole life.

how: Theravada Buddhists chant this Dhammapada verse in Pali at temples and at home, and it is recited at Magha Puja, the full-moon day that remembers the gathering where tradition says the Buddha first taught it.

games.q: what does “the teaching of the buddhas” mean?
o: the closing blessing that monks chant over a new house
a verse that names the path: no harm, the good, a clear mind
a vow the monks make never to break a single rule again

games.q: the verse, line by line — tap the pairs.
p: this is the teaching of the Buddhas

s: the verse is basically a list of things not to do
only the first line is a not. the second takes up the good, and the third clears your own mind.
the third line asks you to empty your mind of every thought
pariyodapanam is making clear, washing clean: clearing what clouds the mind, not erasing thinking.
buddhana is plural: the teaching of the Buddhas
the verse frames this as what awakened ones teach, not one teacher's private rule.

games.q: your little cousin needs 'what Buddhists believe, in one sentence' for a school worksheet, due tomorrow. which line fits the verse?
o: don't add harm, take up the good, and clear your own mind.
sit still and empty your mind until nothing can bother you.
follow the monks' rules and you'll be reborn somewhere nicer.
games.why: the verse gives three moves, in order: stop the harm, take up the good, clear your own mind. it calls that the teaching of the Buddhas.

practice: Chant the whole verse slowly, one line to a breath: sabbapapassa akaranam; kusalassa upasampada; sacittapariyodapanam; etam buddhana sasanam. Rest in the quiet after the last word.
Then chant it once more, a little softer, and let the sit carry the rest.

wordCard.voice: The teaching of the Buddhas: etam buddhana sasanam. Not doing evil, taking up the good, clearing your own mind, in four short lines.

orig.note: Pali, the verse's first line in Devanagari letters: sabba, all; papa, evil; akaranam, not-doing.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart in Pali. Short enough for a car ride, deep enough for a lifetime. Seventeen days of Pali, and counting.

sources.q: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 183 (Pali): sabbapapassa akaranam, kusalassa upasampada, sacittapariyodapanam, etam buddhana sasanam
